title: Roll a covered call down without losing your shares
summary: The stock falls from about $100 to $95 and the sold call is at 80% of its maximum. You can close it as a win, or roll down to a $97 call for $0.90, so the two calls can earn about $2.10 in total. If the stock rallies back to $100, close the short call before assignment. Losing your shares is something you let happen, not something that happens to you.

steps.caption: The stock drops from about $100 to $95. The first sold call is now at 80% of its maximum.
Ahead of the theta schedule: close the first call and keep about $1.20 of profit.
Roll down: sell the $97 call for $0.90; the two calls can earn about $2.10. The chart holds one $97 call sold at entry, not this roll.
The shares still carry the loss from $100 to $95. The calls capture extrinsic value along the way.
The stock rallies back to $100, above the $97 strike. Now the shares are at risk of being called away.
Close the short call before its extrinsic value runs out. You keep the shares; you lose the upside, not the stock.

takeaways: Rolling a covered call down captures more extrinsic value after a drop.
A lower strike lowers the cap on your upside if the stock recovers.
Assignment happens when you let it: close the short call before extrinsic value runs out.
caveats: Several numbers in the transcript are garbled; the $1.20 first-call profit and $2.10 total follow the speaker's example.
Rolling down locks in the share loss below the new strike if the stock recovers.
The chart and tables model one $97 call sold at entry (stock $100, about $5.29), not the roll ($97 call for $0.90 at $95). Their max profit, breakeven and EV belong to that single call.

backtest.note: Monthly 30 delta covered call closed at 80% of max profit and resold; the roll-down step itself is not modeled.
